title: About — Silver Current Press
heading: On Silver Current Press
description: About Silver Current Press: an independent literary imprint in Philadelphia founded by James F. Mulhern.
text: About — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact I · Of the House On Silver Current Press Our Mission Silver Current Press exists to publish literary fiction with the patience and care it deserves. We work slowly, edit closely, and design our books to last. We honor the lineage of Joyce and O’Connor — writers who trusted their readers. We believe the finest books are made by hand, by people who love them, for readers who will keep them. Silver Current Press was founded in MMXXVI in Philadelphia by the novelist James Mulhern, with a single, unfashionable conviction: that literary fiction, made carefully and championed patiently, still finds its readers. We are a small house and intend to remain one — publishing few titles a year, each held to the standard of a book that ought to last beyond its season. Our literary lineage runs through two writers in particular. From James Joyce we take the conviction that the local, properly attended to, becomes universal — that a single street in Dublin or South Philadelphia can hold the world entire. From Flannery O’Connor we take the older, harder lesson: that fiction owes its reader a kind of truthfulness that may not be comfortable, and that grace, when it appears, often arrives armed. James Mulhern is the author of the Kirkus-starred novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams and of Molly Bonamici , Useless Things , and Assumptions and Other Stories . His work has appeared in more than three hundred and fifty publications. In 2015 he was a Fellow at the University of Oxford. He has taught literature for two decades, and he founded this press because he wanted to make the kind of books he had spent his life reading. We believe the best books deserve readers who slow down. Our editorial philosophy is plain. We acquire books we believe in. We edit them closely — line by line, in conversation with the writer, in the tradition that produced Maxwell Perkins and Robert Gottlieb. We design them with restraint, set them in classical type, and put them into the hands of the booksellers and librarians who still read what they shelve. We do not chase trends. We do not pad a list. We do not publish a book we would not be proud, ten years on, to have set our device upon. We accept submissions from agented writers and, occasionally, from writers who have published widely in literary magazines. We answer every query. We say no kindly when we must, and yes only when we are certain. To begin a correspondence, write to [email protected] or use the letter form . For James Mulhern’s own writing, criticism, and selected essays, visit his author site at authorjamesmulhern.com . title: Accessibility — Silver Current Press
heading: Accessibility
description: Accessibility statement for Silver Current Press.
text: Accessibility — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact X · Of Accessibility Accessibility Silver Current Press believes literature should be open to every reader. This site is designed to meet, and where possible exceed, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at Level AA. What we have done Type set at 18 pixels or larger for body text, with line-height generous enough for screen reading. Colour contrast tested against WCAG AA at every typographic level, in both light and dark modes. Light and dark reading modes, toggled at the top right of every page; the choice is remembered between visits. Semantic HTML throughout — proper headings, landmarks, lists, and form labels — so that screen readers may navigate the site with ease. All images carry descriptive alternative text. Decorative ornaments are marked aria-hidden so that screen readers may pass over them. Keyboard navigation across all pages and forms; visible focus rings on every interactive element. A motion-respecting design: animations and reveals are disabled for visitors who have asked their operating system to reduce motion. What we are still working on Accessibility is a continuing practice, not a finished product. If you find a page, a form, or a document that does not work well with your assistive technology, please write to [email protected] with a short description of the problem and we will repair it as quickly as we can, generally within thirty days. Books in accessible formats Each Silver Current Press title is published as a fully reflowable e-book in EPUB 3, with semantic markup, proper heading levels, alternative text on illustrations, and a navigable table of contents. Print editions are set in generously sized type with adequate leading. Large-print editions and audio editions are produced where reader demand and resources permit. Contact for accessibility Accessibility coordinator: James Mulhern · [email protected] . We answer accessibility questions within seven days. title: Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: Currents
description: Currents is the essay series from Silver Current Press: dispatches on craft, reading, and the writing life.
text: Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Vol. I · A Literary Gathering Room Currents A drawing-room of letters from the literary deep. “A book must be the axe for the frozen sea within us.” — Franz Kafka, letter to Oskar Pollak, 27 January 1904 Currents is the press’s gathering room — an ongoing series of short essays on the writers we keep returning to (Joyce, Woolf, Fitzgerald, O’Connor, Hemingway, and the long company of writers they made possible), on questions of craft, and on the books we find worth passing along. Newest entries appear first. Each is a small conversation, not a definitive judgment. Some conversations stay small. Others widen, over time, into the full scholarly studies our authors publish elsewhere — a current finding, eventually, a river. What you will find here: Reflections on the writers we return to — the classics, the moderns, the rooms they made. Notes on the writing life — questions of craft, problems of form. Editorial counsel — advice from the desk on revision, voice, and patience. Recommended reading — books we believe deserve a careful audience. Letters from readers — your own thoughts, selected and lightly edited. Join the Currents Readers are welcome here. If a passage has stayed with you, if you have a question about craft, a book you wish more readers knew, or a thought on one of the writers we love — write to us. Selected letters appear in Currents, attributed by first name and city, or anonymously if you prefer. Send to [email protected] with ‘Currents’ in the subject line. Keep it under 400 words. We read everything and reply to what we publish. By writing to Currents, you grant Silver Current Press a non-exclusive, perpetual right to edit your letter for length and clarity and to publish it on this site and in related Silver Current Press materials, with the attribution you specify. You confirm the work is your own and retain copyright in it. We do not pay contributors; selection is its own honor. RECENT ESSAYS From the Gathering Room Vol. I · No. VI · MMXXVI The Membrane and the Metaphor By The Editors · August 2026 A psychiatrist named Ernest Hartmann spent years studying people with unusually vivid dream lives and found something larger underneath: a measurable range of temperament running from thick-boundaried to thin. What he found in a questionnaire, the Romantic poets had already found in a letter, a coinage, and an ode. Read the full essay → Vol. I · No. III · MMXXVI The Word That Comes Back By The Editors · August 2026 There is a kind of poem that turns on a single word — a word so ordinary it might have gone unnoticed the first time it was spoken. Marie Howe does this in "What the Living Do," where the word is lovely . Frank O'Hara does it in "The Day Lady Died," where the word is practically . What these poems know is that recurrence, in the domestic register, is how grief actually behaves. Read the full essay → Vol. I · No. IV · MMXXVI The Sentence That Refuses to Name Itself By The Editors · July 2026 There is a moment, near the end of any great short story, when the writer could name the thing and does not. The scene arrives at its climax. The reader understands. And then the sentence turns aside, refuses the noun, and gives you a curtain, a window, a train ticket, a shoe. Chekhov taught modern short fiction this move. Every writer who has written a serious short story since has been trying, one way or another, to earn it. Read the full essay → Vol. I · No. V · MMXXVI The Grandmother in the Doorway By The Editors · June 2026 Some writers spend a career going somewhere. Others spend a career coming back to the same place. Faulkner did the second. Woolf did the second. Marilynne Robinson has done the second for forty years and won every prize a writer can win for the going and never-leaving. The recurring figure — the grandmother in the doorway, the lighthouse at the end of the water — is not a failure of imagination. It may be the most disciplined thing a writer can do. Read the full essay → Vol. I · No. I · MMXXVI Fitzgerald, at the Edge of a Sentence By The Editors · April 2026 The ending of Babylon Revisited is one of the great quiet endings in American fiction. Fitzgerald, who rewrote the final paragraph more than once, refuses the consolations a lesser writer would have reached for. There is no flourish, no rounding image. The widowed Charlie Wales is left alone in a Paris bar at Christmas, and the prose declines to comfort him. Read the full essay → Vol. I · No. II · MMXXVI A Book Worth Knowing By The Editors · February 2026 If you have not read William Maxwell's So Long, See You Tomorrow, set aside the hundred and thirty-five pages it will ask of you and give them gladly. It is the story of a murder on an Illinois farm in 1921 and of a boy who, fifty years later, is still trying to write down what he should have said to another boy at school. Read the full essay → Currents is curated by James Mulhern. Selected entries appear quarterly. Letters not selected are read with care and gratitude. The Letters from Readers feature will appear once correspondence is received. — VII — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. text: DMCA Policy — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact XI · Of Notice DMCA Notice Silver Current Press respects the intellectual property of others, and we ask that visitors and contributors do the same. This page sets out our procedure for responding to claims that material on this site infringes a copyright, in accordance with the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 512. Designated agent for notice The agent designated to receive notifications of claimed infringement is James Mulhern. Notices must be sent in writing to the addresses below and must comply with 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3). Designated Agent: James Mulhern, Silver Current Press Email: [email protected] (preferred) Postal: Silver Current Press, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (full address on registration with the United States Copyright Office) What a proper notice must contain Your physical or electronic signature. Identification of the copyrighted work claimed to have been infringed. Identification of the material on this site claimed to be infringing, with enough detail (a URL is best) for us to find it. Your full contact information: name, postal address, telephone number, and email address. A statement that you have a good-faith belief that the use is not authorised by the copyright owner, its agent, or the law. A statement, made under penalty of perjury, that the information in the notice is accurate and that you are the owner or are authorised to act on the owner's behalf. What happens next On receipt of a notice that meets the statutory requirements, we will remove or disable access to the material expeditiously and will, where contact information is available, notify the contributor of the material. We will not provide your contact information to the contributor without your consent, except as required by law. Counter-notification If you believe material of yours was removed or disabled in error, you may send a counter-notification under 17 U.S.C. § 512(g) to the same address, including the elements required by the statute. We will pass it on, and unless we receive notice of a court action, we may restore the material in ten to fourteen business days. Repeat infringers It is the policy of Silver Current Press to terminate, in appropriate circumstances, the access of contributors who are found to be repeat infringers of copyright. A note for our authors Silver Current Press believes copyright should be defended, plainly and at once, when it is infringed. If you are an author published by the press and you find your work pirated on a third-party site, please write to us. We will issue takedown notices on your behalf as part of our continuing care for our titles. text: Privacy Policy — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact VII · Of Privacy Privacy Silver Current Press is a small, single-proprietor literary publisher operated by James Mulhern in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. This Privacy Policy explains, in plain terms, what information this website collects, how it is used, and the rights you hold over it. The press collects as little as possible; the press shares less. 1. Who operates this site Silver Current Press, a fictitious name registered (or being registered) in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to James Mulhern, an individual proprietor. For privacy inquiries, write to [email protected] . 2. What we collect when you correspond When you write to the press through the contact form, by email, or when you submit a manuscript or query, we receive whatever you choose to send: your name, your email address, your message, and any attached file. We retain that correspondence for as long as is needed to respond to it and to keep an orderly editorial record. We do not sell, rent, or trade this information. 3. What is collected automatically Like every site on the open Web, the hosts that serve these pages may automatically log a visitor's IP address, browser type, referring page, and the date and time of the visit. This information is used for security and for understanding which pages are read. We do not run third-party advertising, behavioural tracking, or cross-site profiling on this site. 4. Cookies This site uses a single first-party cookie to remember whether you prefer light or dark reading mode. The cookie holds the value light or dark and nothing else. No analytics or advertising cookies are set. 5. Email and newsletters If you subscribe to the press's newsletter or to our Substack , your email is held by that newsletter platform under its own privacy policy. You may unsubscribe at any time from the footer of any letter we send. 6. Manuscripts and submissions Submitted manuscripts and queries are read only by James Mulhern. They are kept confidential, are not shared with any third party, and are deleted from our records once the editorial decision has been communicated, unless the work has been accepted for publication, in which case files are retained for the duration of the publishing agreement. 7. Children This site is not directed to children under thirteen. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children. 8. Your rights If you live in a jurisdiction with statutory privacy rights — including the European Union (GDPR), the United Kingdom (UK GDPR), and the State of California (CCPA / CPRA) — you may write to [email protected] to request access to, correction of, or deletion of any personal information we hold about you. We will respond within thirty days. We do not sell personal information. 9. Security We use industry-standard encryption (HTTPS) for every page. No system, however, is perfectly secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute confidentiality of information transmitted over the Internet. 10. Changes to this policy If this policy is materially revised, the new effective date will appear below and, where appropriate, a notice will be posted on the home page for thirty days. title: Services — Silver Current Press

description: Editorial services from Silver Current Press: developmental editing, manuscript evaluation, and copyediting for writers.
text: Services — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact II · Of Editorial Practice Editorial Offices The editorial offices of Silver Current Press accept manuscripts from writers preparing work for submission, self-publication, or private circulation. Each project is read by an editor with literary training and a long apprenticeship in the form. We work line by line, in conversation, never by template — the editor’s task is to clarify the writer’s intention, not to overlay her own. I Manuscript Evaluation A diagnostic read of the whole manuscript, delivered as a single editorial letter. No marks in the manuscript itself. Best when a writer wants to know whether the book is working — and where — before committing to a full edit. Deliverable One editorial letter of roughly 4–6 double-spaced pages, in PDF. Included Assessment of premise, structure, pacing, character, voice, and prose; a prioritized revision roadmap; one 45-minute follow-up call within 30 days. Not included In-manuscript margin comments; line-level rewrites; copyediting; proofreading; a second letter. Best for A complete first or second draft when you are deciding what to do next. $650 flat Up to 90,000 words · 3–4 weeks II Developmental Editing The deepest edit we offer — a scene-by-scene reading of the manuscript with editorial queries throughout, followed by a long revision letter. For manuscripts that are asking large questions of themselves. Deliverable Your manuscript in Microsoft Word with tracked changes and margin comments at the scene, chapter, and section level; plus an editorial letter of roughly 8–12 double-spaced pages, in PDF. Included Structural and craft response throughout; one 45-minute call after delivery; 30 days of clarifying questions by email at no additional charge. Not included Line-level rewrites paragraph by paragraph; copyediting; proofreading; fact-checking; a second pass after revision (quoted separately). Best for A complete draft that needs structural work before it can be polished. $0.030 / word 6–8 weeks III Line Edit Sentence-by-sentence work on the prose itself — rhythm, clarity, register, image, and the slow business of finding the writer's truest voice on the page. Assumes the structure is settled. Deliverable Your manuscript in Microsoft Word with tracked-changes edits to nearly every paragraph and margin queries where alternatives are offered; plus a short editorial note of 600–1,200 words summarizing recurring patterns and stylistic choices. Included Paragraph-level revisions; cuts, condensings, and reorderings within passages; suggested rewordings; consistency of voice; 30 days of clarifying questions at no charge. Not included Structural changes or chapter reorganization (those belong to developmental editing); grammar-only correction (that's copyediting); proofreading; rewriting in another voice. Best for A revised, structurally finished manuscript ready for craft-level attention. $0.025 / word 4–6 weeks IV Copyedit Grammar, syntax, usage, punctuation, and house style applied with a light editorial hand. The manuscript's last serious read before it is typeset. Deliverable Your manuscript in Microsoft Word with tracked changes; a one-page style sheet listing spelling, hyphenation, and house decisions made for the book; and a brief cover note. Included Correction to Chicago Manual of Style (17th ed.) unless you prefer otherwise; consistency of names, dates, and recurring terms; light fact checks where errors are obvious; 30 days of clarifying questions at no charge. Not included Rewriting for voice (that's line editing); developmental notes; proofreading after typesetting; comprehensive fact-checking or permissions work. Best for A manuscript that is craft-finished and needs grammatical and stylistic uniformity before design. $0.022 / word 3–5 weeks V Proofread A final, unhurried reading against the typeset page — for the silent errors that survive every prior pass. Deliverable An annotated PDF of the typeset manuscript or laid-out galley with corrections marked, plus a short cover note listing recurring issues. title: Submissions — Silver Current Press
heading: Submission Guidelines
description: Submission guidelines for Silver Current Press. When and how the press considers new work.
text: Submissions — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About The Gathering Room Contact IX · Of Submissions Submission Guidelines Silver Current Press reads with care. Submissions are received only at certain times of year, and only along the routes set out below. These guidelines exist so that we may give your work the attention it deserves, and so that you may know what to expect from us in return. When the gate is open Open submission windows are announced on the home page and in the press's Substack. Outside of those windows, we cannot read unsolicited manuscripts. Solicited and previously requested manuscripts are read year-round. What we read Literary fiction (novels and story collections), narrative nonfiction (memoir, essay, the literary lecture), and poetry of formal accomplishment. We do not read genre fiction (romance, thriller, fantasy, horror, sci-fi) unless its literary intent is clear. We do not read children's books, screenplays, or self-help. How to submit Query first. Send the first ten pages of the manuscript and a one-page query letter to [email protected] , with the subject line QUERY · [Genre] · [Title] . Manuscript on request only. We do not accept full manuscripts at first contact. Send in 12-point serif type, double-spaced, with numbered pages and your name on every page. PDF or DOCX. Simultaneous submissions are welcome. Please withdraw your work promptly if it is placed elsewhere. No reading fees. Ever. What we promise Every query is read by James Mulhern personally. We acknowledge receipt within seven days and answer queries within ninety days. If we ask to read the full manuscript, we will respond within one hundred and twenty days. If we have not written to you within those windows, please write again — your message may have been lost. What we cannot promise We cannot answer specific reasons for a decline, nor offer line-by-line critique in our reply. Authors who wish a detailed reader's report should consider the press's manuscript evaluation service , which is offered as a separate paid engagement and carries no expectation of acceptance for publication. Use of that service neither helps nor harms a future submission. Rights and contract Acceptance for publication is followed by a written agreement. Silver Current Press offers a clear, author-favourable contract: world rights for a defined term, reasonable royalty rates, plain language, and reversion of rights if a title goes out of print. We negotiate openly and answer every question. What is confidential Submitted manuscripts are read only by the press. They are not shared, are not shown to other authors, and are deleted from our records once a decision has been communicated, unless the work is accepted. Your work is your own. See the Privacy Policy for the press's information practices. A final word We are a small press, and we publish few books. Most queries, however accomplished, must be declined for reasons that have to do with the press's slate and resources, not with the work itself. Please take a decline as the partial answer it is, and write again when the next book is ready. — IX — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. title: A Book Worth Knowing — Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: A Book Worth Knowing
description: On William Maxwell's So Long, See You Tomorrow — a small book about a boy and a murder and the memories a writer cannot recover.
text: A Book Worth Knowing — Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Vol. I · No. II · MMXXVI · Currents A Book Worth Knowing William Maxwell's So Long, See You Tomorrow and the confession of what we cannot know. By The Editors · February 2026 If you have not read William Maxwell’s So Long, See You Tomorrow , set aside the hundred and thirty-five pages it will ask of you and give them gladly. It is the story of a murder on an Illinois farm in 1921 and of a boy who, fifty years later, is still trying to write down what he should have said to another boy at school. What makes the novel a quiet masterpiece is Maxwell’s willingness to admit, on the page, the limits of his own knowing. He invents what he cannot remember; he says so plainly when he does. The book becomes a confession of how we tell the stories of people we have failed. It is a small book. We have given copies to more friends than any other novel on the shelf. Each has come back grateful. — The Editors ← RETURN TO CURRENTS — • — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. title: Fitzgerald, at the Edge of a Sentence — Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: Fitzgerald, at the Edge of a Sentence
description: On the restraint of Fitzgerald's Babylon Revisited and how a short clause can carry a grief the story refuses to name.
text: Fitzgerald, at the Edge of a Sentence — Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Vol. I · No. I · MMXXVI · Currents Fitzgerald, at the Edge of a Sentence On the restraint of "Babylon Revisited" and the moral instrument of the sentence. By The Editors · April 2026 The ending of “Babylon Revisited” is one of the great quiet endings in American fiction. Fitzgerald, who rewrote the final paragraph more than once, refuses the consolations a lesser writer would have reached for. There is no flourish, no rounding image. The widowed Charlie Wales is left alone in a Paris bar at Christmas, and the prose declines to comfort him. What does the grief’s work is the moral instrument of the sentence itself — short clauses, plain nouns, the slow turning of the comma. We come back to Fitzgerald not for the parties. We come back for the restraint at the end of the room. — The Editors ← RETURN TO CURRENTS — • — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. title: The Grandmother in the Doorway — Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: The Grandmother in the Doorway
description: On the recurring figure in fiction as method rather than habit — Woolf's Mrs. Ramsay, Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha, and the case for coming back to the same door in every book.
text: The Grandmother in the Doorway — Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Vol. I · No. V · MMXXVI · Currents The Grandmother in the Doorway On recurring figures in a body of fiction — Woolf, Faulkner, and the case for return. By The Editors · June 2026 Some writers spend a career going somewhere. Others spend a career coming back to the same place. Faulkner did the second. Woolf did the second. Marilynne Robinson has done the second for forty years and won every prize a writer can win for the going and never-leaving. The recurring figure — the grandmother in the doorway, the lighthouse at the end of the water — is not a failure of imagination. It may be the most disciplined thing a writer can do. We were reading, again, the middle section of To the Lighthouse — the “Time Passes” passage in which Mrs. Ramsay dies in a single bracketed clause and the empty house is given ten years of a paragraph — and the thing that struck us was not the famous parenthesis. It was the fact that Woolf had already written this woman before, in Mrs. Dalloway , in The Voyage Out , in the earliest sketches. She had spent a career learning to sit with a certain kind of Englishwoman long enough that when she was ready, she could hand her over to death in a bracket and still make the reader mourn her. The bracket is the confidence of long acquaintance. It is the terminal restraint of a writer who has already spent thousands of pages proving the case, and no longer has to. Faulkner did the same with a place. Yoknapatawpha was not a stroke of genius. It was a decision, made in Flags in the Dust and adhered to until his death. To choose to write, again and again, about a single county in Mississippi is to accept, up front, the accusation of narrowness — the same accusation Emily Dickinson accepted about the second-floor bedroom in Amherst, the same accusation Chekhov accepted about the provincial doctor’s house. What the accusation misses is that a writer who returns to the same ground is not repeating themselves. They are learning what the ground can bear. Each new book adds a layer to what the previous book made possible. Sartoris in the first novel is preparation for the Sartoris of Absalom, Absalom! . The reader who has followed him grieves in three dimensions where a first-time reader could only grieve in two. What is at stake here, we think, is the case for recurrence itself. We live in a moment that tells writers — and especially writers who have not yet made their reputations — that novelty is the coin of the realm. Every book must be new. Every voice must be a departure. The MFA workshop trades in the surprising sentence rather than the earned one, and the market rewards the writer who reinvents themselves at every step. We suspect the market is wrong. The reader you want, we think, is the reader who returns to a body of work the way one returns to a house one has known for years. What such a reader wants is not to be surprised by the front hall. What they want is to walk in, hang up their coat, and find the same grandmother in the doorway, saying almost the same thing. The almost is where the whole art lives. The grandmother in the doorway is the writer’s method. Coming back to her is not laziness. It is the slow, honest work of finding out what her doorway means. — The Editors ← RETURN TO CURRENTS — • — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. title: The Membrane and the Metaphor — Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: The Membrane and the Metaphor
description: On psychiatrist Ernest Hartmann's research into 'boundary thinness,' and how it maps onto Keats's negative capability, Coleridge's esemplastic imagination, and Wordsworth's visionary gleam — with a note on our own James F. Mulhern's essay 'Thin Places.'
text: The Membrane and the Metaphor — Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Vol. I · No. VI · MMXXVI · Currents The Membrane and the Metaphor On boundary thinness, Keats's negative capability, and the raw material of a working imagination. By The Editors · August 2026 A psychiatrist named Ernest Hartmann spent years studying people with unusually vivid dream lives and found something larger underneath: a measurable range of temperament running from thick-boundaried to thin. At the thick end, thought stays separate from feeling, sleep is a closed door, the past is filed and finished. At the thin end, sensation and idea arrive together, the border between waking and dreaming goes soft, and the past visits the present uninvited. Hartmann called the trait boundary thinness. He was not, it turns out, the first to notice it — he was only the first to measure it. John Keats got there first, writing to his brothers at twenty-two, trying to name what made Shakespeare Shakespeare. He landed on a phrase: negative capability, the ability to sit inside uncertainty without grasping after a tidy resolution. That is a thick-boundaried mind's discomfort and a thin-boundaried mind's native climate. Keats went further elsewhere, saying the poet “has no self” — that he can pour himself into a sparrow outside the window and peck about in the gravel alongside it. Two centuries before the questionnaire existed, Keats was describing, in a letter to his own family, exactly what it feels like to have very little wall between the self and the rest of the world. Samuel Taylor Coleridge coined a stranger word for the same phenomenon: esemplastic, meaning shaped into one — his term for the imagination's power to dissolve separate things into a single new thing. That is not so different from what happens when a memory and a present moment blend without asking permission, or when a feeling arrives already wearing the shape of a physical object. The Romantics called this imagination. Hartmann, without citing a line of Coleridge as far as we can tell, ended up measuring the same trait with a clipboard. And then there is Wordsworth, who wrote that we come into the world “trailing clouds of glory,” and asked, achingly, “Whither is fled the visionary gleam?” Readers have taken that for two centuries as a poem about the ordinary sadness of growing up. It reads differently once you know that boundary thinness, on average, does thicken with age — that most people's walls harden as they mature, while a smaller number keep something of that early permeability their whole lives. Wordsworth may not have been merely wistful. He may have been reporting a fact: most people lose the gleam, and a few simply don't. We raise all this because our own James F. Mulhern has written directly into this territory, in an essay called “Thin Places,” which takes its title from the old Irish phrase for ground where the wall between this world and the next has worn thin. The essay traces its own private history of the trait — a mentor who named it in him decades before Hartmann's research existed, and gave him, in a single sentence, permission to stop apologizing for a mind that let too much in. We recommend it to any reader who has ever been told, by a teacher or a parent or their own embarrassment, that they feel things too much or notice too much or ask too many questions. The essay's case, and ours, is that this is not a flaw to outgrow. It may be closer to the raw material of the work itself. You cannot write a character from the inside, or build a metaphor that actually surprises a reader, unless something in you is willing to let the borders go soft for a while. The membrane is not a defect. It is an instrument — strung a little more finely than most, built to pick up what a thicker wall would never let through. — The Editors ← RETURN TO CURRENTS — • — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. title: The Sentence That Refuses to Name Itself — Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: The Sentence That Refuses to Name Itself
description: On the small, load-bearing gesture in short fiction of Chekhov and Alice Munro: the sentence that declines to name what the reader has just understood.
text: The Sentence That Refuses to Name Itself — Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Vol. I · No. IV · MMXXVI · Currents The Sentence That Refuses to Name Itself On Chekhov, Alice Munro, and the moral technology of the unspoken. By The Editors · July 2026 There is a moment, near the end of any great short story, when the writer could name the thing and does not. The scene arrives at its climax. The reader understands. And then the sentence turns aside, refuses the noun, and gives you a curtain, a window, a train ticket, a shoe. Chekhov taught modern short fiction this move. Every writer who has written a serious short story since has been trying, one way or another, to earn it. In “The Lady with the Dog,” the moment arrives when Gurov, at last conscious of loving Anna, catches sight of himself in a hotel mirror. Chekhov does not tell us he is in love. He gives us gray hair. It has become fashionable in workshops to call this restraint , but the word is thin. The correct word is ethics . Chekhov refuses to name the thing because to name it would flatter both the character and the reader — would give Gurov the consolation of self-knowledge before he has done anything to deserve it, and give the reader the pleasure of the moral summary they came for. Chekhov denies both. What we get instead is gray hair in a mirror. The story is over. Nothing has been solved. Everything has changed. Alice Munro carries this inheritance across the Atlantic and updates it, in story after story, for the household register of small-town Ontario. Read the ending of “Friend of My Youth” and count the nouns Munro does not use. She refuses forgiveness . She refuses reconciliation . She refuses peace . Instead she gives us a dream, an old woman named Flora walking down a road, a possibility that the dreamer’s mother might, at last, have been the one who did not deserve the story her daughter had been telling about her all her life. The reader is left with a debt they can never pay and a story they cannot forget. That is not restraint. That is the exact opposite of restraint. It is a maximum act, achieved by declining to say the maximum word. We call this, in workshops we teach and in books we recommend, the moral technology of the unspoken. It is difficult to teach. It cannot be taught by rule. It can only be taught by long attention to the writers who have done it — and by the writer’s slow, painful realization that the sentence they have just written explains too much, and by the willingness to strike it out. What Chekhov and Munro share — across a century, across two continents, across every difference of milieu that ought to separate them — is the conviction that the reader is capable of arriving at meaning without being led there by the elbow. That is the deepest form of respect a story can offer a reader. It is also, we think, the deepest form of love a writer can offer a character: to decline to summarize them. The story that says everything says less than the story that says almost everything and then, at the last possible moment, turns its face to the window. — The Editors ← RETURN TO CURRENTS — • — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora. title: The Word That Comes Back — Currents — Silver Current Press
heading: The Word That Comes Back
description: On the way a single word can travel through a family, from door to hospital bed, and become the load-bearing beam of a poem. With a note on our own Copacetic.
text: The Word That Comes Back — Currents — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon SILVER CURRENT PRESS Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Home Catalogue Services Journal Currents About Contact Vol. I · No. III · MMXXVI · Currents The Word That Comes Back On recurrence in a poem, a family, and a life — with a note on our own "Copacetic." By The Editors · August 2026 There is a kind of poem that turns on a single word — a word so ordinary it might have gone unnoticed the first time it was spoken. Marie Howe does this in “What the Living Do,” where the word is lovely . Frank O’Hara does it in “The Day Lady Died,” where the word is practically . What these poems know is that recurrence, in the domestic register, is how grief actually behaves. You do not remember your father in oratorical Latin. You remember him because he used to say copacetic before every long car ride, and now the word arrives in a hospital room forty years later and nearly finishes you. Repetition, in the received schoolroom account, is a rhetorical device. In the household economy of a real family, it is closer to a sacrament. A word repeated by one person over decades becomes an occupied territory. It becomes a way of saying, without ever saying it, that everything is not fine and that the person saying it cannot afford to admit so. Which is why, when the word comes back — from the doorway of the family kitchen into the doorway of a hospital room — it does more work than any twenty new words would do. The old word arrives with its whole history intact. We will note, since it belongs to this press and we can, that our own James F. Mulhern has written such a poem. It is called “Copacetic,” and it appeared in Academy of the Heart and Mind in February 2020. It begins with a child’s word game — The word of the day is copacetic. — and it ends, after a hospital scene the poem earns and does not overexplain, with a line that we have watched him revise across drafts: When I wake, I find that he has gone. An earlier draft read At dawn, he was gone . The revision is small and enormous. It moves the moment of loss off any objective, Easter-morning stage and places it inside the speaker’s own waking, where the empty tomb has been relocated into the private morning of a grieving man. We admire the poem for many things — the doorway rhymed against the doorway, the blue bathrobe, the restraint of the ending — but the revision is the tell. Restraint of that kind is not a temperament. It is a decision, made and remade, sentence by sentence. What we take from all this, for our own reading and writing, is a small rule that has served us well: when a word comes back, ask why . Ask what it was doing the first time, and what work has been added to it in the interval. Ask whether you, as the writer, are the one bringing the word back — or whether the word has come back on its own, from the underground water table of a family, and asked you to make room for it. The poems that last, we think, are the ones where the writer had the humility to make room. — The Editors ← RETURN TO CURRENTS — • — Silver Current Press · Philadelphia · Established MMXXVI silvercurrentpress.com © MMXXVI All rights reserved Privacy · Terms · Submissions · Accessibility · DMCA · Author Set in Cormorant Garamond & Lora.
